items.title: Ozone hole one of the largest in decades
items.snippet: In contrast to the 2025 seasonal ozone hole above Antarctica, which was the fifth smallest since 1992, this year’s ozone hole ranks as one of the largest in 48 years.

items.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
items.snippet: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

items.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
items.snippet: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.

items.title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
items.snippet: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.

items.title: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean
items.snippet: The deep sea has long been considered a safe haven for marine life, but new genetic research suggests a hidden biodiversity crisis may be unfolding far beneath the waves. Scientists analyzing more than a decade of genetic data from five species of deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf discovered troubling signs of extinction risk in every species examined.

items.snippet: Interstellar space is the scene of active chemical processes: molecules form there in the gas, but also on the surface of tiny dust grains covered in ice. items.title: Learning facts out of interest may take less mental effort than learning them for money
items.snippet: When completing tasks or acquiring information, humans can be driven by intrinsic and extrinsic motivations. The term intrinsic motivation entails doing something because it is interesting to us or we find it enjoyable, while extrinsic motivation means doing it to obtain a reward, such as money, praise or a good grade.

items.title: Two mechanisms of amino acid transport in a rare disease-associated protein revealed
items.snippet: Cells must constantly exchange amino acids with their environment to make proteins and support numerous bodily processes. To do this, they have specialized transporters located in their membranes.

items.title: Scientists discover quasar formed within a mere 630 million years of the Big Bang, setting a record
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

items.title: Early Stone Age rock carvings in Scandinavia may have been signposts for hunting grounds
items.snippet: Between roughly 9,000 and 4,000 B.C., artists in ancient Scandinavia painstakingly carved large, sometimes life-size images of elk, reindeer, bears and other creatures into rock faces teetering on the edge of fjords, rivers and lakes. But their meaning has long been debated.

items.title: Sensory deterrents aren't a 'one-size-fits-all' solution for sharks and rays
items.snippet: A study on how select species of rays and sharks respond to sensory deterrents has reinforced why there isn't a one-size-fits-all solution to prevent fisheries bycatch.

items.title: Many buyers willing to pay more to know where their food comes from
items.snippet: New research from Curtin University reveals many Australians are prepared to pay more for food when they know where it comes from and how animals are treated, despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures.

items.title: Mathematics fact fluency interventions for students with mathematics difficulties
items.snippet: Associate professor Jonté Myers knows that developing fluency with mathematics facts is key to mathematics proficiency. However, many students struggle to develop these foundational skills.

Beautiful People Divorce More. Why?
items.snippet: Being attractive makes dating easier. Keeping a relationship may be another story. Research has found links between higher physical attractiveness and shorter relationships, with one possible reason being simple. Attractive people often have more potential alternatives. Dating apps make that problem much bigger. They turn thousands of people into an endless stream of choices, creating decision fat
